solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable copy, its numbering matching the numbers printed in it and the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Old travelling salesman put an end to crooked pedlar not having line right (12, two words)

indicators.note: something crooked is bent out of true, so the letters are bent into a new order
the line is not kept but has a right put in its place, one abbreviation swapped for another

parts.note: to scotch a rumour or plan is to put an end to it
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line; it is the letter that leaves
R is the abbreviation for right; it is the letter that comes in

explanation.surface: A dodgy pedlar of old is driven out of business, minus a line of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the L of PEDLAR for R to get PEDRAR, then rearrange it. To scotch is to stamp out or stop.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scotch draper was a historical itinerant credit trader who took orders door to door rather than carrying stock.

clue.text: Crumbs round desert nut-tree

indicators.note: round says one piece goes about the outside of the other, wrapping it

parts.note: both crumbs! and coo! are mild exclamations of surprise
to desert a post is to quit it

explanation.surface: Someone eats a few crumbs from a nut tree out in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumbs' looks like a noun, bread fragments, but it is the dated British exclamation of surprise, like 'goodness!'.
explanation.definitionFit: The coquito is a Chilean palm which bears small edible nuts, hence a nut-bearing tree.

clue.text: Almost two metres is required to intercept kick

indicators.note: to intercept is to cut into the path of something, so one piece cuts into the middle of the other

parts.note: to toe a ball is to kick it with the toe end of the foot
taken as written

explanation.surface: A football tactic: a run of nearly two metres is needed to cut out a kick.
explanation.definitionFit: The toise was an old French unit of length of about 1.95 metres, so just under two.

clue.text: Pistol whip?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a revolver from the famous American maker
second meaning: as a verb, to beat with a knotted rope's end

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pistol whip' reads as one act, striking with a gun butt; split, the two words each define the answer separately.
explanation.definitionFit: A Colt is a make of revolver, and to colt is an old verb for thrashing someone with a rope end.

clue.text: Legal bits of religious text: vast number found in ditch

indicators.note: found in says one piece is located inside the other

parts.note: a ha-ha is a sunken ditch serving as a fence round a park
a lac or lakh is the Indian word for a hundred thousand

explanation.surface: A huge number of sacred legal texts are dumped in a ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a ditch with a wall in one side, a landscape-garden boundary that keeps livestock out without spoiling the view.
explanation.definitionFit: Halacha is the body of Jewish religious law drawn from the Talmud, the legal parts as against the narrative ones.

clue.text: In —— one has … Armenian dosh possibly

definitions.text: In —— one has … Armenian dosh possibly

indicators.note: possibly hints at one of several arrangements, so the letters may be put in a different order
the blank stands for the answer: added to the other words it makes up the full set of letters, so those words must be taken away

parts.note: the full set of letters, taken as written
taken as written, letters to remove
taken as written, letters to remove

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank sentence about what money an Armenian might have.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus IN ONE HAS rearranges to ARMENIAN DOSH, so strike those letters and A, R, M, D remain. Read whole, the clue also defines: in the blank one has Armenian money.
explanation.definitionFit: The dram is the currency of Armenia, and dosh is slang for cash.

clue.text: Ray, a giant, chucking out a loose rock

parts.note: ray or re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: chucking out is throwing away, so one letter is thrown out of the word

parts.note: Goliath was the Philistine giant slain by David
the letter thrown out

explanation.surface: A giant flings a loose rock at a ray, as in a fable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ray' looks like a fish or beam of light; here it is the musical note, spelt RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Regolith is the layer of loose, broken rock and dust lying over solid bedrock, as on the Moon.

clue.text: The other Indian tree with a pungent smell

parts.note: the poon is an East Indian tree whose wood was used for masts
a tang is a sharp, pungent taste or smell

explanation.surface: Of two Indian trees, the second gives off a strong smell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other' seems to pick out a second tree, but it is the coy British phrase for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Poontang is American slang for sexual intercourse, which 'a bit of the other' also euphemistically means.

clue.text: Tourist met wandering round fringes of Mount Hawke?

indicators.note: round says the rearranged piece goes about the outside of the other
letters that go wandering stray from their places and end up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the fringes of a phrase are its two edges, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the place name

explanation.surface: A tourist is met roaming the outskirts of a village called Mount Hawke.
explanation.walkthrough: Mount Hawke is a village in Cornwall, which is the point of the question mark: Cornish locals call visitors emmets.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmet is a dialect word for an ant, used in Cornwall for the swarming summer holidaymakers.

clue.text: Dim fellow to show contempt for (about last, literally)

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes about the outside of the other

parts.note: to boo someone is to jeer at them in contempt
literally means in letters: the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A put-down: a slow-witted man is scorned for always coming last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literally' asks for the last letter of the alphabet rather than a word meaning last.
explanation.definitionFit: Bozo is American slang for a stupid or foolish man, a dim fellow.

clue.text: One whose morals have lapsed lacks bride, being wild

indicators.note: wild letters are out of control and scatter into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man with loose morals stays single because he is too wild.
explanation.definitionFit: A backslider is someone who relapses into bad habits or sin after reforming.

clue.text: Regular AZ event, first of clues obviously meriting prizes

indicators.note: first of asks for the opening letter of each following word

parts.note: initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Describes Azed's monthly clue-writing contest, where obviously good clues win.
explanation.walkthrough: AZ is Azed himself: his clue-writing competitions run regularly, and the prizewinning clues are those described.
explanation.definitionFit: Comp is informal shorthand for competition, and Azed sets a clue-writing contest each month.

clue.text: P-paradise pierced by furrow, becoming commonplace

parts.note: the stammered first letter, taken as written

indicators.note: something pierced has another thing driven into it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Eden is the paradise garden of Genesis
a stria is a fine groove or furrow

explanation.surface: A stammering speaker says paradise has been ploughed up and made ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'P-' imitates a stammer and gives its letter as written, ahead of the paradise word.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrian as an adjective means dull and ordinary, lacking inspiration.

clue.text: Holiday home by creek one painted yellow (possibly wrongly)

parts.note: a villa is a rented holiday house abroad
a gio or geo is a narrow creek or gully in Orkney and Shetland

explanation.surface: A holiday villa by a creek has had its walls painted yellow, maybe badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellow' looks like paint colour but means cowardly; the bracket hints that the word itself is a corrupt Shakespearean form.
explanation.definitionFit: Villagio is a Shakespearean coward, a garbling of Italian vigliacco, so one called yellow, possibly by mistake.

clue.text: Hill ridge in e.g. Texas, south, unusually acute on sides

indicators.note: a piece placed on both sides of another surrounds it
unusually means not in the usual way, so the letters do not stay in their usual order

parts.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A geography note: a Texan hill ridge to the south rises at an unusually sharp angle.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuesta is a ridge with one steep face and one gentle slope, a word used in the American Southwest.

clue.text: Was grumbling appendix initially caught by Doctor Edmund?

indicators.note: something caught by another is held inside its grasp

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, an army doctor

indicators.note: initially points at the opening letter only

parts.note: first letter
Ned is a pet form of Edmund

explanation.surface: A patient complains whether a doctor called Edmund has spotted their appendicitis.
explanation.definitionFit: To moan is to complain or grumble, so moaned is the past tense, was grumbling.

clue.text: SE European prison with extra-large facilities

parts.note: jug is slang for prison
OS stands for outsize, the clothing size
the facilities is a euphemism for the toilet, the lav

explanation.surface: A prison in south-east Europe boasts outsize amenities.
explanation.definitionFit: Jugoslav is an older spelling of Yugoslav, a native of the former Balkan state in south-eastern Europe.

clue.text: It describes leafy appendage arils put out

indicators.note: letters put out are thrown out of order and laid down anew

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Botanical jargon: the seed coverings called arils grow out like leafy outgrowths.
explanation.walkthrough: An aril is a fleshy covering on some seeds, a decoy botanical term here used only for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stipular is the adjective for a stipule, the small leaf-like outgrowth at the base of a leaf stalk.

clue.text: RC headgear plenty will appear in and the rest rejected

indicators.note: to appear in something is to be seen inside it
something rejected is sent back, so it is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: etc, et cetera, means and the rest
a lot means plenty

explanation.surface: Catholic hats appear in quantity while the remainder are turned away.
explanation.definitionFit: A calotte is a skullcap such as the zucchetto worn by Roman Catholic clergy.

clue.text: Shows disapproval about king, retrograde, creating disturbance among Scots

indicators.note: retrograde means moving backwards, so the result is read back to front
about means around, so one piece goes about the other

parts.note: to tut is to click the tongue in disapproval
R is short for rex, king

explanation.surface: Someone tuts at a backward-looking monarch, and a Scottish commotion follows.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into TUTS after the first T, and the whole is then turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Sturt is a Scots word for strife, trouble or a disturbance.

clue.text: Main characters in famous play? Run is including e.g. Gielgud

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: including means taking something in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: taken as written
Val Gielgud was a BBC radio drama producer, brother of Sir John Gielgud

explanation.surface: Asks who leads a famous play's run, which includes a member of the Gielgud acting family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gielgud' suggests the actor Sir John, but the first name needed is that of his brother Val.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rivals is Sheridan's famous comedy, and its leading characters are indeed rivals in love.

clue.text: Undersized roll, this, flaky

parts.note: to roll and to run are both to move along smoothly, as a wheel does

indicators.note: something flaky falls apart in pieces, and the pieces reform in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A baker holds up a small, flaky bread roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll' and 'flaky' set up a pastry scene; roll is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: A runt is the smallest of a litter, so runtish means small and stunted.

clue.text: What's spare and lush, reared in e.g. conservatories?

parts.note: spare and lean both mean thin, with no excess fat

indicators.note: in a down entry reared means raised up, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a lush is a drunkard, as is a sot

explanation.surface: Asks what thin, lush plants are grown in places like conservatories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spare and lush' reads like a description of greenery; both words are synonyms for people instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A conservatory built against a house wall with a sloping roof is a typical lean-to.

clue.text: Arcade that is Italianate today in CA city

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: Los Angeles, a city in California (CA)
oggi is the Italian word for today

explanation.surface: An Italian-style arcade appears today in a Californian city.
explanation.definitionFit: A loggia is a gallery or arcade open on one side, a feature of Italian architecture.

clue.text: What's held (from either end) in elaborate netting

indicators.note: from either end says the word reads the same whichever end you start from
in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Something caught in ornate netting, whichever way you look.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle someone holds; it comes from Latin for 'he holds'.

clue.text: Particular 'number'? I appeal for help given different sort of number

parts.note: taken as written
SOS is the distress signal
a PIN is a personal identification number

explanation.surface: A song, a particular 'number', is a plea for help with a different number in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks show 'number' is not a song: it is a quantum number of a particle.
explanation.definitionFit: Isospin is a quantum number in particle physics treating the proton and neutron as states of one particle.

clue.text: The first person (French) in court produces swabbing aid

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: to court and to sue both mean to woo, and to sue is also to take to court
je is French for I, the first person

explanation.surface: A French speaker in a lawsuit produces a mop.
explanation.definitionFit: Sujee or soogee is a soapy cleaning mixture sailors use for scrubbing decks and paintwork.

clue.text: Sandbank that makes salt going about stop, as before

indicators.note: going about means going round, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: sal is the chemist's Latin for salt
ho is an obsolete word for a stop or halt; 'as before' marks it as old

explanation.surface: A sandbank forms where salt deposits around an old stopping point.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoal is a shallow place in water, a sandbank.

clue.text: Loveless couple, daft (I'd omitted quarrel)

indicators.note: love is zero in tennis, so being without love drops a round letter

parts.note: a duo is a couple

indicators.note: the pair of letters is left out of the word before

parts.note: daft means stupid

explanation.surface: A daft couple has fallen out of love, and an argument follows.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is O, from tennis scoring, so DUO loses its O; STUPID loses ID.
explanation.definitionFit: A dust-up is an informal word for a quarrel or brawl.

clue.text: Small port edging Louisiana plain?

indicators.note: edging something is forming the edges round it, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: Pt is the abbreviation for port
LA is the postal abbreviation for Louisiana

explanation.surface: Asks whether a little harbour on the Louisiana coast lies on a plain.
explanation.definitionFit: Plat is an old word for a flat piece of ground, hence a plain; the question mark flags the less common sense.

clue.text: Oily paste: lid turned over to enclose one

indicators.note: turned over means flipped end to end, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: lid is slang for a hat
to take something in is to enclose it
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Instructions for a jar of oily paste: flip the lid and seal one inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lid' looks like a jar top but is slang for headwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahini is a paste of ground sesame seeds, rich in oil, used in Middle Eastern cooking.

clue.text: In infinite space it's around most (or least) distant orbital point

indicators.note: turned around, the letters are read in the opposite direction
In says the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An astronomy line: out in endless space lies the furthest or nearest point of an orbit.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse or apsis is either of the two extreme points of an elliptical orbit, nearest or furthest from the body orbited.

clue.text: Sweet lozenge kept in reserve? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: quite the reverse says the whole result is to be read backwards
something kept in a store sits inside it

parts.note: a pool is a reserve held in common, as of money or workers
a lozenge is a tablet or pill

explanation.surface: A sweet lozenge is kept back for later, or perhaps the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite the reverse' sounds like a contradiction of the scene, but it reverses the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A lollipop is a boiled sweet on a stick.

clue.text: Gather judge again withholding praise

indicators.note: withholding something is keeping it back, so those letters are left out

parts.note: to reappraise is to judge again
taken as written, the letters to drop

explanation.surface: Someone collects a second verdict but holds back the compliments.
explanation.definitionFit: To reap is to gather in a harvest.

clue.text: Put a cross beside impulse transmitter

parts.note: taken as written
a cross is the letter X
on can mean beside, as in a house on the river

explanation.surface: Mark a cross next to the part that sends nerve impulses, as in a biology test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put' is the instruction to write the pieces down one after another.
explanation.definitionFit: An axon is the long fibre of a nerve cell that carries impulses away from it.

clue.text: Still bothered by seven fifty threes

indicators.note: bothered means stirred up and upset, so the letters are disturbed

parts.note: taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is still troubled by seven, fifty and threes, like a puzzled arithmetic student.
explanation.definitionFit: Still as an adverb means however or even so, the same as nevertheless.
